opus-5.5.text:
I think the clearest evidence is that we're already seeing it, in small ways. When you train a single model on a large, diverse mix of robot data, many different robots, many tasks, many environments, and you add the semantic knowledge that comes from pretraining on web data, you start to see the model do things nobody specifically demonstrated. It follows a new instruction it hasn't seen paired with that motion. It handles an object it never touched in training. It recovers from a mistake in a way that wasn't in any one trajectory. None of that is magic. It's recombination. The model has seen pieces of the behavior in different contexts and learns to put them together.

That's the same thing that happened with language models. Nobody wrote down every essay a language model can write. The model learns the underlying structure well enough to compose new things. My bet is that physical behavior is also highly compositional. Grasping, pushing, reorienting, and inserting, combined with an understanding of what objects are and what people want, gets you a very large space of behaviors from a much smaller set of examples.

The second part, which I think matters even more in the long run, is that robots aren't limited to imitation. Imitation learning gets you roughly to the level of the data, plus whatever generalization you get from composing it. But a robot acts in the world and sees the consequences. That lets you use reinforcement learning, or at least some form of autonomous improvement, where the system practices, gets feedback, and gets better than its demonstrations. We've seen that in narrower settings for a long time. A robot can learn to do a task faster or more reliably than the human teleoperator who showed it. The interesting question now is how to do that at scale on top of these big pretrained models, so the prior gets you into the right ballpark and real-world experience takes you past it.

So I'd put it this way: broad data gives you generalization through composition, and interaction gives you improvement beyond the data. Language models mostly had the first. Robots can have both, and I think that's ultimately why robot learning could go further than people expect.

r001.rationale: It says diverse robot data teaches behavior pieces that the model can recombine to perform things nobody specifically demonstrated, including new instructions and object interactions.

r002.rationale: It mentions recovery from an unrepresented mistake in general, but does not report a robot righting a tipped shopping bag.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think the thing to appreciate is that the behaviors in the training data aren't really the thing you're learning. What you're learning is something more like an understanding of how the physical world works, and the behaviors are just the lens through which you get at that. If I have a robot that's seen thousands of hours of people folding laundry, cleaning up kitchens, putting things in drawers, the individual tasks are not that interesting. What's interesting is that in the process of fitting all of that, the model has to figure out that cloth deforms in a certain way, that objects don't pass through each other, that if you push something it moves and if you let go of something it falls. Those are regularities that cut across all the tasks, and once you've internalized them, you can recombine them in ways that nobody ever demonstrated.

We saw hints of this even in the early work. With RT-2, for instance, you'd train on fairly mundane pick-and-place data, and then you could ask it to move the apple to the number that's the sum of two plus one, and it would do it. Nobody collected that. What happened is that the vision-language backbone had some semantic understanding, the robot data taught it how to connect that to actions, and the composition came for free. The more recent stuff with pi-zero and pi-point-five pushes on this harder. You take a robot into a home it's never been in, with a kitchen layout it's never seen, and it can still tidy up, not because that kitchen was in the data, but because the generalization is happening at the level of concepts, not at the level of trajectories.

I'd draw the analogy to language models, with the obvious caveat that the analogy is imperfect. Nobody would say GPT-4 only does the things that were in its training set. It saw a lot of text, and from that it extracted a kind of model of how ideas relate, and now it can write things that are not in the corpus. The reason people have been skeptical that this works for robots is that the data is so much smaller and the signal is much noisier. And that's fair. But I think the skepticism gets the mechanism wrong. The question is not whether you've demonstrated every task. The question is whether you've seen enough diversity that the cheapest explanation the network can find is a genuine model of the world rather than a lookup table. Once you're in that regime, the behaviors you get out are not bounded by the behaviors you put in.

And then the other piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that the robot can keep learning after deployment. A language model gets its data and that's it. A robot is physically in the world. It can try things, see what happens, and improve. So even if you're worried that the initial training data caps the capabilities, that cap isn't permanent. Reinforcement learning on top of a good pretrained policy means the robot can go beyond what any human demonstrated, because it's optimizing against reality, not imitating a person. That's really the long-term bet. The demonstrations get you a foundation, and then experience takes you past it.

r001.rationale: It says diverse experience teaches cross-task regularities and that the model can recombine them in ways nobody demonstrated, with novel-task examples.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of arithmetic-directed pick-and-place and tidying in unfamiliar homes, but does not mention spontaneously righting a tipped shopping bag or the absence of deliberately collected recovery data.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we should distinguish between learning from data and copying the behavior in the data. If you train a system to imitate, then you’re asking it to reproduce the actions that somebody took. There can still be generalization there, but reinforcement learning gives you a different mechanism: you’re asking it to find actions that lead to a good outcome.

Imagine a robot has experience opening a cabinet, and separately it has experience picking up objects. Nobody has demonstrated opening that particular cabinet and retrieving an object from inside it. But the experience could contain enough information to figure out how to do that. The resulting behavior is new, even though the pieces that make it possible came from prior experience.

And that can go beyond combining skills. If you learn enough about how your actions affect the world, you can potentially discover a better way to accomplish a task than the ways represented in your data. That’s part of what makes reinforcement learning interesting: the behavior that generated the experience doesn’t have to be the behavior you ultimately learn.

The big caveat is coverage. If your data tells you nothing about what happens when you take some action, you can’t just assume that optimizing against a learned model will produce the right answer. It might produce something that exploits the model’s errors. So this isn’t a claim that any fixed dataset can give you arbitrary capabilities. You need sufficiently broad experience, and ideally the ability to try things, observe the results, and improve.

But deliberately collecting a demonstration of every behavior you want is a much stronger requirement than collecting experience from which those behaviors can be learned. I think that distinction is where a lot of the potential lies.

r001.rationale: The response explains that prior experience with opening a cabinet and picking up objects can be composed into the novel behavior of retrieving an object from that cabinet, without a demonstration of that exact sequence.

r002.rationale: The response does not report a robot spontaneously righting a tipped shopping bag or say that recovery behavior was absent from deliberately collected training data.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we should distinguish between collecting examples of a behavior and collecting the ingredients from which that behavior can be learned. If you watch someone solve a task, you’re seeing one particular sequence of decisions. But what you could learn from that experience is much broader: how objects move, what happens when you grasp something, which actions are likely to succeed in a particular situation.

Suppose a robot has learned to open drawers and it has learned to pick up objects. You might ask it to retrieve an object from a drawer, even though nobody demonstrated that exact task. There’s no fundamentally new physical skill there, but it has to put what it knows together in a new way. That’s already a capability beyond the behaviors deliberately demonstrated.

Now, that doesn’t happen automatically. If you train a system just to reproduce the actions in a dataset, it might learn a very narrow mapping. The more interesting question is whether it learns enough about the consequences of its actions to choose different actions when the objective changes. Reinforcement learning gives you a mechanism for doing that: the demonstrations can provide a starting point, but the objective is successful outcomes, rather than matching the demonstrator.

And if the robot can collect additional experience, it can try things that weren’t in the original data and improve on them. The human doesn’t need to know how to perform every behavior we want the robot to discover. We need to provide enough experience to get learning started, and a way to determine whether it’s making progress. The hard part is making that process reliable and practical in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot can combine learned drawer-opening and object-picking skills to retrieve an object, although that exact task was never demonstrated.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe a robot spontaneously righting a tipped shopping bag without deliberate training data.
